utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Tom Hannis with case manager Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and our intern Mr. Miroslav Cuskic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is nothing that need -- yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do it now or I can do it after I finish my last question. I have spoken with the Defence about certain documents. I have five payroll-type documents. I think we have an agreement that I can tender those without further questions to the witness. And then there are a series of documents that are called daily bulletins of various types that I would propose to tender without any further questions to the witness. There are three of them that I will show him because there are three different kinds of daily bulletins based on the source, where they come from, and I have agreed with Mr. Zecevic in order to do that that none of those that I'm tendering have a signature of Mico Stanisic. Some have no signature. Some have a typewritten Mico Stanisic with no signature. Some have his typewritten name and a signature by somebody else, sometimes with the word "za" and sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Dealing with the daily bulletins first, I assume from what you say has passed between you and counsel for the Defence that the relevance of these is patent?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my primary purpose in offering these is to show that there were contemporaneous reports about things that were happening in the region at the time and to show that that communication was -- went up and down within the MUP and outside the MUP. The contents of many of them aren't significant for me at this point, but to establish the fact of communication, the regularity of communication, and the persons with whom communications were made is the purpose in offering this group of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is anything that the other side -- any comment that the other side has to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have definitely a different view on the subject, but I don't think that it would be appropriate at this point that we -- that we state our position on that. But in any case, we are not objecting under the circumstances, as Mr. Hannis have said, that is, we don't have objection of -- we don't object that those are the authentic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the -- in terms of the daily bulletins, do I understand your position to be that your -- your objection is not -- you have no objection to the authenticity of them, but the secondary question is whether there is any issue as to the fact of these communications. Because as I understand Mr. Hannis's explanation, he isn't going to seek to argue that the content is particularly helpful; it's merely the fact of the system of communications. And I'm wondering whether that is in controversy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as I said, the authenticity we don't challenge. The contents, we -- we want to rely on the contents because the contents show what the ministry in fact knew about the facts in the field. It's very simple. Of course we intend to rely on the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of the two categories of documents, we would admit the bulletins, but not the payrolls because we're not persuaded that those additional payrolls - bearing in mind that one was admitted yesterday - are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then I will perhaps try and make a bar submission later and point out the specific reasons why I think particular ones are relevant, and I'll move on and not bother to deal with it today. Thank you. I will -- to save time I'll list the daily bulletin 65 ter numbers at the end rather than now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you've answered the question I was about to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So long as we don't lose sight of something that has to be done today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'll try and be sure and do it before I sit down with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I'll remind the witness that he's still on his oath. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic. I'd like to start by showing you a document that is 65 ter number 2516, and this is a rather lengthy document so maybe I can hand you a hard copy of the B/C/S. This is a document that you will have looked at during proofing. Can you tell us what it says on the cover page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says security services centre, the acronym is there, CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now if we could go to the next page in B/C/S and keep the English page that's up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This in my English translation appears to be a list of sent and received dispatches, and column 1 says "sent by, number, and date." And the first entry says "SMUP BiH ..." Is that the MUP headquarters? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should mean the Serbian MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where on April 22nd and 23rd would that have been located? Would that be in Vrace or Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should have been in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you, Mr. Kezunovic, I need you to find the page that has entry number 13 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In e-court I think it's two pages further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you recognise the signature that's at the far right-hand -- in the far right-hand column for entry number 13?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be Pejic R, standing for Radovan probably, because there was a Radovan Pejic among the employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. I wanted to ask you if you knew a - I thought it was Radomir - Radomir or Radovan Pejic who worked at the communications for CSB Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's a signals man that is operator, that is Radovan Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And looking at this entry under the column where it says "reply received from -- reply received from who, number, and date," we see what appear to be a series of telephone numbers. Do you recognise those numbers and what -- and know what they might be associated with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only recognise network groups by the prefix. For instance, I can say the first number belongs to Banja Luka, the second one Sarajevo, the third one to Bijeljina, this one to Trebinje, and the final one to Doboj because this is the prefix of the number, the calling code for the city. As for numbers, the actual telephone numbers, I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you see in addition to the CSBs for Banja Luka, Sarajevo, Bijeljina, Trebinje, and Doboj, this one was also sent to the staff in Pale? And what's the last one. It does not appear to have been put in the English translation, but in your B/C/S copy there's a last entry next to a telephone number. I'm sorry, that's -- I think that refers to the next item, number 14. Can you tell me what that -- what those two entries are under number 14. Is it Pale staff -- do you find that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What does that say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "staff Pale," but what kind of staff, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And underneath that, what does that next one say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vlada," meaning government, but I can't see the rest. It says "government BH," but I can't see what comes first before that. It could be SR. It is probably SR. "The government of the SR, Serbian Republic, of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could zoom out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are we able to discern from this document the nature of the items that were received?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was it phone calls, or was it dispatches or letters? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm going to try and link up a couple of these to help illuminate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 13 we see is listed as 01-26 dated 26-04-92. And the summary of contents says it's the supplement memo 01-18/92 dated 20 April 1992 regarding reception of workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go briefly and put up on the screen Exhibit P1420 to see if we can make a connection between that entry and a document. And if we could zoom in on the top half.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see that on your screen, Mr. Kezunovic? This appears to be 01-26/92, dated 26 April 1992, to the five CSBs. And right below the CSB heads it says: "In accordance with: Our act number 01-18/92 from 20 April ..." Would you agree that this appears to be the document that is referred to in item number 13 of the log?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would ask to go to page 10 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for you, sir, on your hard copy, if you could go to the last -- item number 49. You'll see on -- and I'm not sure what page that is in the B/C/S in e-court, but you'll see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we leave this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To -- is this -- was this document received at the CSB or was it sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm hesitant to say certain things in front of the witness, but we've seen that this says it was sent by -- from the ministry and the dispatch is sent to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right, right. So it was sent from the ministry? That's the way we should understand this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and you'll see the fax header on this particular document is "Srpska Republika BiH MUP."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. It was just because I was led to believe that the log-book was of the log-book -- the CSB Sarajevo log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So why would --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm getting right to the point to try to explain that, Your Honour. That's why we're going to item number 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see item number 49, Mr. Kezunovic, appears to be the last in a series of entries of documents that were sent by the MUP headquarters or from MUP headquarters, and there's a line drawn across the last three rows that seems to indicate that that's being closed out in some fashion. Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we need one more page in the e-court, one page further on. And if we could go to the bottom -- oh, I'm sorry, one more page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did -- I'm sorry, did you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was waiting for my turn. I agree that this has been underlined and that it ends with a period, and that on the following page a new chapter is being opened for the SB CSB, and it should be -- mean "next" -- or rather, that this book was used up until this period where the line is drawn as a log-book of the communications centre, which was also the communications centre used by the Ministry of the Interior and the CSB of Sarajevo. And that from that time on it was divided and continued to function as the log-book of the CSB. This probably relates to the initial period at Vrace, where there was one communications centre catering to two organisational units, the ministry and the CSB. But I'd like to make another mention here and that is that in the heading, in the title, it says "sent and received dispatches." Now, in the communications centre separate log-books are kept for sent dispatches and received dispatches, both coded and open ones. And in that first period we did not have the same types of books or one book where the communications centre such as Vrace were functioning. So somebody found one of these protocol books and used it, put it to use good use, and kept the records with this type of book. So that was at the beginning, in the first period. We have log-books which differ if you look at the columns inside. It was only at the end of the year that we managed to print a united, single log-book, a uniform log-book, that we sent out to all the centres. So at the beginning there might have been these different books, but that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I don't have the correct B/C/S page in e-court to show you what I want to show you. Witness, can I ask you to read out at the top of that page you're looking at, there should be an eight-digit number that's printed or typed. Can you read that page for us so I can get the computer on the right page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on my translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Do you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's page 10, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, it is page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does it appear that these first 49 entries in this book are actually dispatches that were sent? None of them are received items but they're all sent items?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes I would say so, I would say that too. That's why I told you that it says in the title. "Sent and received," but in actual fact it relates to those sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last entry number 49 in this part of it is dated 13 May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of May, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, your next page shows just simply CSB Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the following page for you, the next page in e-court, please, in both English and B/C/S -- well, I think that's the end of English because we only translated those portions relating to MUP headquarters. But for the first page after CSB Sarajevo we see now the numbers start with the number 1 and the first item is dated 14 June it looks like; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From your earlier answer I understood you to be telling us that in the beginning April and early May, MUP communications centre in Vrace shared space with the CSB Sarajevo communication people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's only in formal terms. The communications centre was one, the same people working in it, whereas the function, that is to say to whom that centre served, as I said we shared it with MUP and the CSB of Sarajevo. So there was one centre, the same installations, the same people working for two organisational units, distributing dispatches and receiving dispatches from two organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it appears that after May sometime this log-book was taken over and used exclusively by CSB Sarajevo communications people? You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you in the MUP headquarters communications personnel move to Pale approximately and set up business there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an exact date, but I can give you the sequence of events chronologically. A decision was taken, first of all, that the security centre should relocate from Vrace to Lukavica, and at the time those of us who belonged to the MUP returned to Pale. As I say, I can't give you a date. I don't remember, but chronologically speaking that's how things evolved when that decision was taken. That's when the employees of the CSB moved to Lukavica and those of us who were in the MUP returned to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And apparently after 13 May you must have had a different log-book you were using for sent dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we continued to receive and send out dispatches through the communications centre, which was at Pale. Because as I said earlier on, almost half of the leading people in that official period was at Pale and the other half were at Vrace --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and as I say, that's how the Pale centre in Pale came to be formed, and then it continued working for the requirements of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we had a miscommunication. My question was: After May 13th then when you were working in Pale you must have had a different log-book in which to enter sent and received dispatches?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically speaking, this book in physical terms, the book we have in front of us, the one you're pointing to, was transferred to a new location which was the CSB. And the line was drawn under that and CSB was written, security services centre, and then they continued to use that book in the centre exclusively as a book of records of the communications centre of the security services. Now, the book that was physically used at the MUP in Pale functioned normally. It was just that the users, those from the MUP who were at Vrace, joined up and sent their dispatches via that centre at Pale too. But what you asked me about the exact date when I transferred, I don't know, and here's why I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as somebody who was -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I need to stop you. I'm -- I have limited time and so I need to move on. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document. I just gave one example where we matched up an entry in the log-book with some documents that we already have in evidence. There are others, but I -- unless Your Honours require, I can indicate them to you or I can do that later. But I need to try and move on and get some of the other things in I want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so it's -- admitted and marked, the -- that's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the log-book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- log-book, thank you. The name has escaped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the 65 ter or the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was 65 ter 2516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 2516, thank you. Oh, yeah, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kezunovic, I want to ask you next just about a question about Sokolac. Did you know a man named Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware of a unit that was referred to as the Sokolac unit or the police platoon from Sokolac of which Mr. Malovic was the commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know about the police station at Sokolac and the policemen working in that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know about Mr. Malovic and a group of men he commanded in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the following about him, that he originated from the area, he was born there, he worked in the army, and he did service somewhere in Croatia. That's what I heard -- not from him, but that's what people said. And that after the withdrawal from Croatia he was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, who he belonged to exactly, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean in organisational terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you not see him in and around Pale in 1992 when you were working there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of uniform did he wear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was some kind of camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anything unusual about the particular camouflage uniform that he wore that distinguished it from other camouflage uniforms you saw in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that when I first saw him on one occasion he was wearing the customary type of uniform, our uniform - and when I say "our," I mean the one that was used from before. Now, later on he had this kind of camouflage uniform which -- well, what can I say? It was a sort of combination of black, grey, white, I don't know how to describe it actually. Perhaps a uniform suited to winter conditions, let's say, although I have seen those same uniforms on television of late in police forces throughout the world in different areas, the same or very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you now about tab 84. This is 65 ter 3218. I can hand you a hard copy of this one as well. Thank you. This appears to be another sort of log-book. I just have a couple of questions about this one. The left column which is entitled in my English translation "postal number and date" has a series of numbers beginning with 10-2/92. Can you tell us anything about that series of numbers, what that would refer to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes. It's the number from the document that we mentioned yesterday, the nomenclature, and how all the internal organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior were designated; that is to say, the document originates from some of those organisational units or a organisational unit that had that number to designate it, number 10-26 probably in line from 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it says dash 93 and if it's all 1993 then I assume that's what it is in that whole column, the date sent, 21st of March, 1993, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the page that I'm looking at, the first row is scratched out. Is that what is on your hard copy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 2, 10-2/92, my date says 09-November-92?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my copy it says 10-26/93.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see the computer screen. I may have handed you the wrong page. Can you see on the computer screen that these appear to be all 1992 entries, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could have the hard copy back and see what I've handed him. I see. It was upside down. You had the last page first. And if you could go to item number 24. I think it's maybe the third page for you. You see in the far right there are a series of signatures. Are you able to recognise any of those signatures as anyone you know or worked with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the signatures of the operators in the communications centres. I never received anything in writing from them for me to be able to follow their signatures and see their signatures, but at all levels if the last level was the CSB they had their team leader and he communicated on their behalf so that I really can't recognise their -- I don't know their signatures. If I knew which organisational unit this belonged to and remembered some of the names, then perhaps I might be able to recognise the signatures and read them. But just looking at the signatures without knowing whose book this is, what organisational unit it belonged to, I really can't. It's practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understood in proofing that you -- I thought you understood that you were able to read some of the names. Even though you might not recognise the signature, you were able to read the handwriting and identify that as a person that worked in your communications centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is this. For example, I can see "Zoka." "Zoka" can only be Zoran. Now, which Zoran is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about item number 30, Todor C. And Zoka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoka, yes, same thing, Zoka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Todor? All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It says "Todor." It does say "Todor."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go back to the first page and just a couple of questions about some abbreviations or acronyms. On the first page item number 3, it says "dispatch 'SS-W-U.'" Can you tell us what those letters stand for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SS is, in fact, a teleprinter mark for the S diacritic Sh letter, and the other is very urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what would Sh be, the SS, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coded, encrypted, "sifrovano."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we mark this for identification, Your Honours? I think I might be able to tie it up with a future witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1429 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the last thing I want to ask you about, Mr. Kezunovic, is yesterday we were talking about some of the meetings you attended where Mr. Stanisic was speaking, and I asked you about one where paramilitaries were discussed. You talked about a group that was in Zvornik and by whom you were actually stopped on one occasion when you were travelling that route, and you couldn't remember the name of the group. I have a copy of a portion of your tape recorded interview with the Prosecution in 2004, where you're talking about that. If I could hand it to you and ask you to take a minute or two to read it, the portion that I've marked, I will ask you a question when you finish reading it. Don't tell me what it says. Just tell me when you've read it and then I'll ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, while we are waiting, we would alert you that you would exhaust your time when we take the break at 10.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to be done before that with any luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now that you've had a chance to read it, did that refresh your memory about the name of the group that you encountered in Zvornik, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I could remember the man better if you described him, or rather, the man in -- at the head of that unit -- well, actually I could remember him better. He had very specific hair, whether it was blond, sort of golden blond or russet coloured. Anyway, they called him Zuco. Now whether that's the man, I don't know, or if that's the group because I saw him on an elevation on a hill above the road with the sun behind him, so I don't think I could remember his face either, but I do remember this characteristic hair colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But apart from that, having read that, did that refresh your memory about what the name of Zuco's group was or what they were referred to as, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, someone who dealt with this problem -- I mean, I read hear "ose," wasps, but I cannot claim anything for a fact because I didn't know any one of them and I didn't know the group as a group. If you have a witness who knows --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that such a group operated in that area, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now and show you Exhibit Number 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, and my learned friends, what I'm going to do is show three different types of daily reports just to show the difference between three kinds that are within the bunch I hope to tender when I finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Three types of daily reports varying according to the source basically. So the first one is 65 ter 952, it's located at tab 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, do you know the person whose name appears at the bottom of this document, Spasoje Camur?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a man like that existed, but I had no particular relationship with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he worked in the department for crime prevention?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the title indicated in the heading, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the crime prevention department issuing daily reports in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure that I was aware. It's possible that between them they introduced this practice, but I really don't know. If you mean only that department and that line of work, it's possible that they introduced this practice because even I in certain periods that were critical for communications introduced at one point the practice that certain centres should send daily reports as long as the problem persisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is this a daily report from the State Security Service of the MUP or of CSB Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe this is from the crime prevention department in the MUP headquarters, an internal type of daily report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who were the addressees of these reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know. I see none on this document so I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why don't we ask the witness and see -- I mean, the interesting issue, of course, is whether Mr. Stanisic received this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can ask him but I assume -- do you know who this document would have been sent to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You're right that there is no addressee indicated, although every document should indicate the name of the sender and the addressee. The heading should indicate who created the document, and in the subheading, which in this case is bulletin, there should be an indication of for whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, do you know if these daily reports, which I assume would come out every day, whether they were sent -- whether they were sent up to the minister's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that, but since you see in the heading "crime prevention department," it sounds the most logical that he was reporting to his administration; and then perhaps the chief of that administration would report that to the minister because he must have known why he had ordered these bulletins to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could next look at 65 ter 953, it's at tab 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, this is a different type of daily report. You'll see this one's dated the 13th of May, 1992, and it says "Serbian Republic of BH Ministry of Interior, Sarajevo, operations duty."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It appears that this comes from a duty operations officer named Nedo Sevo. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he worked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know before the war he worked in that school, the police school in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I used to see him there in the early days of the war while I was at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see that the distribution on this daily report is listed as going to MUP staff and archives. Who was MUP staff as referred to here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to ask you -- because you frequently refer to the MUP staff looking over these past few documents. I don't know about any MUP staff. I know that there is the seat of the ministry where there is an operations duty officer who handles dispatches that they need to send somewhere, but there is no such thing as the MUP staff. There was only at the staff of the special brigade later when the special brigade was established. A staff is something that is established in extraordinary situations in the MUP and a staff exists in the army, but not normally in the police. So I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you as head of the administration for communications receive these types of daily reports from the operations duty people? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was chief of administration, that is to say assistant minister, and I did not receive this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last one I want to show you is 65 ter 951. It's at tab 37. And it's dated the 12th of May, 1992, Serbian Republic of BH, Ministry of Interior, Sarajevo, daily report. And on the last page we'll see it has Minister Stanisic's typewritten name and there's a signature but it appears to be "za." It appears to be for him by someone else. By chance do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive or see these kinds of daily reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if I could go back to the -- the log-book that we looked at at the beginning of your testimony this morning. Just one question about those types of daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I forget what exhibit number we gave this. I think it's 1428.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just in terms of where those bulletins were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at two pages further on I think in the English. I need to see entry number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see that? Entry number 10 is the 25th of April, 1992, daily events bulletin number 6. You see it is listed as being sent to "SRNA." What was "SRNA?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian News Agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And SNA, do you know what that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be an acronym. The Serbian News Agency, "SRNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And "Pale CB." What does CB stand for, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't have any further questions for the witness at this time. I want to read out the list of proposed daily bulletins I'd like to tender at this time. I can do it while he's in the courtroom or while he's out - as you please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, whatever's the most efficient way that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, how many are there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 17, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registry would assign the numbers if you would provide them with a list. That seems to be the most efficient way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll provide a list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Kezunovic, in the MUP, the Republic MUP of the Socialist Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, you spent most of your career as man number one in the administration for communication and cryptographic protection; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that post of man number two in this administration you occupied until mid-1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Moreover, from the multi-party elections until mid-1991, I was even acting chief of administration, so I was practically number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means from sometime in 1990, that is, the multi-party elections until mid-1991 you were acting chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You've told us, I believe it was yesterday, that your post according to this agreement among the political parties was assigned to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then a certain Akif Sabic arrived and told you that from that moment on your services were no longer needed in the Ministry of the Interior and that you should go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. To be more precise, the day when he arrived, assistant minister for staffing affairs Hilmo Selimovic, invited me to his office, informed me that that man was appointed chief of administration, that I should take him for a tour and make him meet the people, show him the equipment. And a few days after that tour, the man invited me to his office and told me that within an hour I should be gone but that I should first inform him where I was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have more than 20 years of service in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 1st of March, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is 13, 14 years?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14. I was into my 15th year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, such behaviour -- I mean, the conduct of this Akif Sabic, was not appropriate to the institution where you were working or any laws or regulations. It was his personal insistence that you should pack up and go look for another job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was not appropriate. First of all, it was not up to him to decide such things or to enforce them. Only the minister could properly make a decision, and even then stating reasons why I should be removed from the ministry. And the minister could do that only if I was guilty of a serious breach or violation of regulations. And that is why I had such a violent reaction to what he said, and we almost got into a fist-fight because I was really fed up by that time. It was less than a year from the multi-party elections, and people had been appointed during that period without any professional qualifications only because the party wanted them in a certain post. And then when somebody was appointed chief of something, they would bring his own equally unqualified people, and it became a conveyer belt. It was happening every day. You would wake up and find a new colleague and somebody would just tell you who they were. We were constantly living in some sort of uncertainty, anxiety, thinking what could possibly come next, and it also concerned my personal life and my family. And that's why I went then to the head of personnel, telling him that I want to hear what's going on. I want it said to my face. And the chief of personnel told me, "Don't you worry, you just do your job and stick to it," but I had nothing to stick to. Nobody gave me any work, nobody asked me for anything. I was just sitting there idly, drinking coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So to sum up, although you remained in the MUP you were practically sidelined and completely excluded from all operational work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course during all that time I was completely marginalised. I had no information about what was going on, and I was not alone in that position. There were several of us in the same position who discussed this among us, and I can't say I was totally in the dark; on the contrary, I had informal but very good information about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This completely disrupted situation in the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina began, if I understood you correctly, just after the multi-party election, and every national party was in a tug of war with the others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of them with equal strength. Some had a stronger pull, and people did things in different ways. Some were sneakier than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if you're moving on to something else perhaps we should take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you, as presently advised, consider that you would need the full four hours that you had requested for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I believe I might be a bit shorter, but I cannot say at this point because I'm just entering the cross-examination. It depends on how the witness will -- you see that the witness tends to give longer answers. So I will try to control him as much as I can and finish within three hours, but I cannot promise that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems -- the reason for asking is whether we are likely to be going into Monday with this witness, and that seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that is -- I discussed with Mr. Hannis and my colleague Mr. Krgovic, and it is definitely going to be a case that we will split into Monday -- spill into Monday, I'm sorry. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, at the end of -- since you wouldn't have completed at the end, when we rise for the day, could you let the Chamber have five minutes before we adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kezunovic, we left off when you said that some of those parties were more persistent in relation to others. Now, I assume you mean that -- or rather, that it is your position and testimony that the Party of Democratic Action, that is to say the Muslim national party, was the most persistent along those lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, is it not, that the situation deteriorated considerably and especially after Mirsad Srebrenkovic's arrival to the post of assistant minister; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that's the time when - how shall I put this ? - this uncontrolled employment in numbers began, especially of Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, at the end of 1991 already it was evident that a joint MUP, given the present situation, would find it difficult to continue to exist and work normally; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is correct because in principle everybody hid information from anybody -- everybody else and everybody worked within a small circle and on the tasks and assignments that suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the interests of the national party that appointed the person to the post first and foremost; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could you just remind us or maybe I could put this question directly to Mr. Kezunovic. When exactly was it that you were sidelined and told that you should leave your position and hand it over to this other gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the moment that that new head of department was nominated and appointed, and he was brought in as a member or a carder of the SDA. So at that point in time. And you can check the date out. I really can't tell you the date, but it was certainly in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Somewhere in the fall of 1991 I understand? Or was it summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly, both are possible. I really can't say now. I didn't try to remember, didn't think along those lines anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's all right. Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you remember that a situation of that kind was recognised by the European Community plan which was known popularly as the Cutileiro Plan at the beginning of 1992, or rather, that the plan envisaged the division of MUP on ethnic lines. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps in the most general terms, but I really can't speak to you about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, yesterday on page 11.582 of the transcript -- well, you were asked by my learned friend Mr. Hannis something relating to Mr. Jesuric from Bijeljina. Do you recall that? Do you remember him asking you that with respect to Predrag Jesuric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me if I knew who he was, who the man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Predrag Jesuric came to be chief of the Bijeljina security station in 1991. He was appointed by the minister Alija Delimustafic, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think he was appointed before the war, but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 11.535 of yesterday's transcript, you said that at the beginning of April 1992 members of the Serbian people and members of the Muslim people had barricades or check-points along the road from Sarajevo towards Pale and Sokolac, do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion you said that that upset the traffic along that road and that buses weren't able to pass?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that but I'd like to just add this. The situation when the barricades were erected led to the interruption of traffic along the road, but that didn't last for a long time. Now, as for check-points, that went on for quite a long period of time. And what I mentioned was with respect to my trips from Sokolac to the other place. This was done by the Green Berets, so I would have to come earlier and wait for one of the buses going in the direction of Sokolac, and they would come up to me several times, search me, ask me where I was going, ask me to identify myself, and I actually had to hide my ID identifying me as a MUP member because it happened that their own Muslims when they saw that these people had ID MUP cards they would confiscate their weapons because that particular person was not perhaps a member of the SDA. So things like that happened along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let me get this right if I understood you correctly, let me just summarise for the transcript. Even before April - and we can say perhaps March 1992 - the Green Berets, that is to say members of that Muslim paramilitary group, had check-points controlling traffic by the Assembly building in Sarajevo, which is in the close vicinity of the bus station, so that every time you went to catch a bus at the bus-stop you had to pass through this check-point where they searched you, asked for your identity and credentials. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a little different. It wasn't a classical check-point. Quite simply -- well, nor was it a bus station. It was just that buses setting out from the bus station which was near the railway station in Sarajevo would pass by that way going east. They would stop if they saw there were passengers, so they would stop by the Assembly building just for a brief stop if they saw you putting up your hand and wanting to board. So they would -- the buses would stop, take in the two or three passengers, and drive on, and that's where the members of the Green Berets were, not like a classical check-point that you had to stop there and have a person take your credentials and so on. They would just be around there 24 hours, round the clock, day and night. And just as they would recognise me and ask me where I was going every time, I remembered them. So that happened before March as well. So let me get that straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were these people armed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that initial period, no. Maybe they had side-arms, pistols, but not anything else -- at least I didn't see any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, if I understood your testimony correctly, you weren't a member of any national party, you were a member of the League of Communists; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists and I left the League of Communists before those elections at an official meeting that was held because it was decided at that time that party work or political work could not evolve within the frameworks of state organs, and up until that like it was only the League of Communists that existed in state organs. So at the time, and this was a little strange as far as I was concerned, people were asked to declare publicly which organisation they wanted to go to on the ground, in the field. And to be quite honest and sincere here, and I want to state this here and now, that in my opinion that League of Communists is most to blame for the disruption of Yugoslavia, and I tore up my party membership book and gave it back. And that's how my party affiliation came to an end and later on I didn't join any other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, sir, how did you declare yourself in ethnic terms, national affiliation, how did you declare yourself, as a Serb or a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My national affiliation, I declared myself as a Serb. And as far as citizenship was concerned, a nationality, I said Yugoslav. And in all the forms that you had to fill out and all the records kept when you gained employment, you would have this citizenship column, and that was SFRY; and then national affiliation, that's the other column you had, and I declared myself as a Serb. You didn't have to declare yourself in terms of any republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, on page 11.534 of the transcript yesterday you said that every year during your work over a period of 14 years in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that every year you would attend training courses for the work that you were doing, specific training courses for your specific job, and that in that way you became acquainted with the latest state-of-the-art technology in the sphere of telecommunications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, do you consider yourself to be a true professional and an expert in the field of telecommunications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you were called sometime in mid-April by Mr. Mico Stanisic and offered the job of heading the department for communications and encryption in the ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you considered yourself ready and able to perform that duty; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And may I make an additional comment to that? First of all, that was one possibility. The other possibility was for me to be mobilised as a recruit, a conscript. But I went to the infantry school for reserve officers, and as such the army would have liked to have me as an infantryman. And since I wasn't a member of any party and all the other circumstances that I described to you, I was very grateful to Mr. Stanisic for giving me this opportunity, first of all, to do the job I did best and it was more comfortable - if I can put it that way - and less dangerous. And I didn't have to go through all the subsequent events that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your testimony correctly, the communications centre attached to the seat of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the course of 1992 was -- well, in actual fact changed its seat and headquarters four times; is that right? First of all, it was at Vrace and then for a brief period in Lukavica, and then it went to Pale, and then from Pale sometime at the beginning of December it was relocated to Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not the communications centre in the physical sense that people moved. It was only from Vrace that we left, but this referred to the centres that had already been established and were operational. They just took on this function of work, of working for the Ministry of the Interior at the headquarters and centre. Let me give you an example. The Bijeljina communications centre, it was in existence ever since the municipal SUP building of Bijeljina existed, and then later on when the organisation changed and you had the MUP and the security centre then I would send cadres to that centre and equipment and documents for them to be able to work for the purposes and requirements of MUP. So that was the sense of that whole operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the main point was that you as head of that department went that way from Vrace to Lukavica, from Lukavica to Pale, from Pale to Bijeljina, that was the route, your route; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on page 11.545 of yesterday's transcript, lines 22 and 23, when asked -- well, you were saying how your telephone lines at Vrace had been cut, and then my learned friend asked you whether it was possible to use the ultra short-wave communications to convey messages. And you said: "Yes, we could do this by relay."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because this part was not properly recorded in the transcript. I'd like you to explain what you meant by "relay."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that an individual who has a radio station transmits an information, a piece of information, to another individual who has a radio station, and the two stations have to have mutual optical visibility. And then the information is passed on in the same way. In some cases it was practiced for several reasons, but not widely. First of all, because it was open traffic and confidentiality of information was not guaranteed, but this mode could be used for brief reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the same page, line 24 and 25 of the transcript of yesterday, my learned friend asked you whether people were able to organise themselves to deliver documentation, for instance, from Vrace to Pale, and you said they were able but you have no idea whether they actually did. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But let me make this quite clear, if I may, in a broader sense. It's one thing to assign someone and organise a service for the entire institution and it's quite another matter when I organise this service for my particular line of work because it wouldn't necessarily suit everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 11.553 my learned friend asked you about a courier service, and you then confirmed that you had not organised such a service and that in your opinion in order to organise such a service it would have been very difficult because you would have needed people, vehicles, petrol, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, Mr. Kezunovic, isn't it, that early in 1992, and especially in the months from April through October 1992, you were facing constant shortages of fuel, personnel, and means of transportation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And just to illustrate let me tell you something that people will probably find incredible. There was one period when the shortages were so bad that the ministry in its seat would ration fuel among its organisational units. I got for my administration 20 litres in one of those months for the month, that is one jerrycan, and I immediately assigned this fuel for the power generator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So for the whole month you got 20 litres of diesel for the entire administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the whole of my administration, just 20 litres for the month. It's incredible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly - and again you've discussed this with Mr. Hannis, but let's be completely clear - I want to ask you about the types of telecommunications at the Ministry of the Interior. One, you had telegraph communications in the form of teleprinters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean generally speaking in the ministry before the war what the police used? Yes, perhaps not in that order, but yes, one network was the teleprinter network.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now this telegraph/teleprinter network, there are documents that were transmitted openly and others were encoded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, dispatches were encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There were also dispatches that were sent through open communications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to explain graphically this technology, this method of work, the communications centre would receive a document written on a type-writer. The operator at the teleprinter re-types the document on the teleprinter, and if it goes through open traffic such a teleprinted document is transmitted on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If the document is encrypted, then this document after being re-typed on the teleprinter goes through the operation of encryption, and only after encryption is it transmitted to the addressee?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the recipient receives that encrypted document they must have a key to decrypt it and the key must be agreed with the sender?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Another type of communications available to you were telephones?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Telephone communications were public and special telephone communications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the latter was called the police network which we called special lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The whole point of these special lines was that this platoon -- sorry, this cable was quite separate from the public telephone cables owned by the PTT.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have to explain. In the entire network of telephone cables from Sarajevo towards centre and from these centres to public security stations, the PTT built up its own system of network, either through cable or through radio relay systems. And in this overall capacity of channels a certain amount was allocated to the police, and the police of course financed it proportionally. Physically they used the same route, but it was also quite separate physically so that one system did not have access to the other one. And in cities, we had a special system. There was a network of our own special cables between all police buildings and installations, and in every city we had our own separate telephone network -- telephone switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, the essence is this: The PTT telephone lines and your own special telephone lines go through these same cables, the same conduits?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they follow, they run along the same physical route.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thus, if PTT telephone lines break down along this physical route, then automatically the special and all the other lines are also broken down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one option. It depends on what the breakdown is about. If it's a general power cut, an outage, then we are all without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then there can be no communication along these routes if there is no electricity. These same telephone lines, the public lines, serve as a conduit for the fax signal; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if the lines are broken down because there is a power outage, then fax communication is also impossible; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of fax communication, you said that it was the position of your service that this line of communication is open and you were very reluctant to use it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that we were reluctant to use it. Before the war it was even forbidden -- sorry, during the war it was even forbidden, but then it was also unnecessary because all the fax communication could also be sent by telephone lines. Perhaps it would not be a bad idea for me to add something to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, say what you want to add and then we'll perhaps correct the -- your answer on the transcript. It was not quite properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The teleprinter network made possible also the so-called circular work. That means we were able at any moment to send a dispatch to all the organs on the ground simultaneously. And we would call it a circular. The contents of all the dispatches that must be sent to all our organs, all the centres, or even municipal stations. And then it would be sent in one single moment, these moments were defined, and it was a very comfortable way to do it. The operator sitting at a disk like this would use these -- this simple telephone switchboard, the kind where you see in movies where they plug a jack into a row of holes, that's how they would send dispatches in this circular. So faxes were of no interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What we've been discussing over the past ten minutes all relates to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the normal functioning of the MUP before the war; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you were talking about the regimen of communication. In the Ministry of the Interior there is an internal regulation specifying exactly what type of documents may be transmitted in the open and which type of documents must be encrypted on a compulsory basis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the main reasons for this distinction between open and encrypted had to do, first of all, with the contents, the information transmitted in the document; and second, the sender and the receiver?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that was irrelevant. It -- the only criterion was the confidentiality and the importance of information transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you just started setting up the communications centre of the MUP in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you had no part of that equipment that you normally had at the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 11.562 when you were shown a document containing the conclusions of the meeting of the 11th of July dealing with nomenclature, namely, numeric designations of various units in the MUP of Republika Srpska, a dead-line was given, the end of July, for this nomenclature to be completed. That means, in fact, that until the month of August 1992, you did not have any official nomenclature in the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it even better, we did not have an established organisation. It was a work in progress. Things were being added or removed all the time or relocated. It was logical, first of all, to draft the rules on internal organisation, and then based on those rules to develop a nomenclature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that the rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska was enacted only in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the date, but I know that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can express myself figuratively, let me say that in actual fact you started setting up communications centres or a communications centre attached to the seat of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with a green light?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was told to go there and to start working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. On page 42, line 24, I used the term "from scratch." I said "green grass," but meaning "from scratch;" is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if I understood your answer correctly, you were told to create a system of communications centres attached to the MUP headquarters which would be operational; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I was told was, "You know what needs to be done best, so go ahead."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Without a doubt -- well, there's no doubt that especially in the first months when you started working to form a communications centre attached to the seat of the MUP, that your communications with the CSBs on the territory of Republika Srpska were non-existent or very often interrupted; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the situation was much worse than you're depicting, and here's why. You say that I was supposed to set up a communications centre. What I was actually supposed to do was to ensure the establishment of a system where this MUP communications centre would be able to function. So that means that even if somebody had equipment and manpower, they didn't have the necessary documents to start working, the encryption, work-plans, and so on. The system is far more complicated than it appears to be at first glance. Setting up a communications centre is just a part of the job. Even if I'm given all the manpower and equipment I need, I need to have all the encryption documents and create a whole system. So it's a little difficult to answer your question in general terms, could this have been possible or not. So when I say "yes, it was possible," but I had to struggle to ensure that all this functioned and also I had to see that the system was not abused in the meantime, that people should not make mistakes sending out information in the wrong way. So that was a broader explanation of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the crux of the matter is this. Let me try and summarise. Not only did you have to set up a communications centre attached to the MUP seat, but to create a whole functional system of communications with all the security services on the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was the difficult part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, for us to establish this functional link between the communications centre attached to the MUP seat and the security centre in Banja Luka, for example, you physically had to go to the Banja Luka CSB with the documentation that you had and took with you from Pale - let me take that example - or from Bijeljina to establish a functional, operational communications system; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is, sir, that if I take the Banja Luka CSB as an example, you arrived at that only after the corridor had been opened, probably in July or August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is, and I think that I've already asked you this and that you said that it was in Brcko that you had to wait for three days in a car to be given permission to drive on to Banja Luka; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the truth is that a normal communications system only became operational after August or during August 1992 with the area covered by the CB -- CSB of Banja Luka and the Doboj CSB; is that right? Could you repeat your answer. It wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, it is also a fact, is it not, that it was only after going to Bijeljina at the beginning of December 1992 and the formation of the communications centre in Bijeljina that that was the beginning of a relatively normal functioning of the system of communication on the territory of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you made a comment and said that in your opinion throughout 1992 everyone just disrupted -- went about disrupting things, including the communications system. Nobody built anything or did anything.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was true of all systems, the electricity supply system and everywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
